claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a solidified solid solution.
FeNiCrMn is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi by removing Co.
The temperature- and strain-rate-dependent strength–ductility balance is governed by the interplay between stacking-fault energy and activation of dislocation slip versus deformation twinning.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi moderately increases stacking-fault energy.
The increased stacking-fault energy caused by Co removal suppresses deformation twinning.
The increased stacking-fault energy caused by Co removal favors dislocation slip.
Suppression of twinning in the Co-free alloy is especially important at low temperatures and high strain rates.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will exhibit lower strain hardening at low temperatures and high strain rates.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will exhibit lower ductility at low temperatures and high strain rates.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will exhibit less deformation-twinning activity.
The strength of Co-free FeNiCrMn will remain similar to or be slightly lower than that of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The hypothesis is applicable to single-phase FCC solid-solution FeNiCrMn alloys from cryogenic through elevated temperatures and at strain rates up to 10^3 s^-1.
Similar or greater twinning activity, strain hardening, and ductility in Co-free FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi at low temperatures and high strain rates would falsify the proposed mechanism.
